metadata.title: Symmetry Transition Preserving Chirality in QCD: A Versatile Random Matrix Model

nodes.name: Universality
nodes.statement: The wide applicability of RMT is referred to as \textit{universality}.

nodes.name: Robustness of spectral statistics against the matrix-element distribution
nodes.statement: Empirically the spectral statistics of physical systems is quite robust against variations in the distribution of matrix elements. The global symmetries of the system have the biggest impact to these statistics.
nodes.statement_short: Spectral statistics are empirically robust to the matrix-element distribution; global symmetries dominate them.

nodes.name: Altland-Zirnbauer tenfold classification of symmetry classes
nodes.statement: There are just ten symmetry classes of Hermitian operators (including RMT) as proven by Altland and Zirnbauer~\cite{AltZirn}.
conclusions: There are just ten symmetry classes of Hermitian operators (including RMT)

nodes.name: Chiral random matrix $\mathcal{D}$ (Osborn-type two-matrix model)
nodes.statement: In the present work we wish to consider the chiral random matrix \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathcal{D} =\left(\begin{array}{cc} 0 & iW \\ iW^\dagger & 0 \end{array}\right), ~ W= H_1+i\mu H_2,\\ H_1,H_2\in{\rm Herm}(N)\ \text{and}\ \mu\in[0,1]~~~ \end{split} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Block off-diagonal Dirac matrix built from $W=H_1+i\mu H_2$ with two independent Hermitian matrices and an interpolation parameter $\mu\in[0,1]$.

nodes.name: Gaussian weight $P(\mathcal{D})$ of the two-matrix model
nodes.statement: distributed as \begin{equation} P(\mathcal{D})= \frac{1}{2^N \pi^{N^2}}\exp\left[-\frac{1}{2}\tr(H_1^2+H_2^2)\right]. \end{equation} Here ${\rm Herm}(N)$ denotes the set of Hermitian $N\times N$ matrices.

nodes.name: Partition function $Z_N^{(N_{\rm f})}$ with $N_{\rm f}$ dynamical quarks
nodes.statement: The partition function with $N_{\rm f}$ dynamical quarks with masses $m_1,\ldots,m_{N_{\rm f}}$ is then given by \begin{equation} Z_N^{(N_f)} = \int d\mathcal{D} P(\mathcal{D})\prod_{f=1}^{N_{\rm f}}\det(m_f \id_{2N} +\mathcal{D})\,. \end{equation} The differential $\mathcal{D}$ is the product of all real independent differentials of $H_1$ and $H_2$. The normalization ensures that $Z_N^{(0)}=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Matrix-model partition function weighting the Gaussian measure by $N_{\rm f}$ quark determinants, normalized so that $Z_N^{(0)}=1$.

nodes.name: Interpolation of the level statistics between GUE and chGUE
nodes.statement: For varying $\mu$ the level statistics of $\mathcal{D}$ interpolates between GUE \cite{Verbaarschot:1994ip,Mehta_book} at $\mu=0$ and chGUE~\cite{Shuryak:1992pi,Verbaarschot:1993pm,Mehta_book} at $\mu=1$. Since these two limits are characterized by different patterns of flavor symmetry breaking [i.e., $\U(2N_f)\to \U(N_f)\times\U(N_f)$ at $\mu=0$ and $\U(N_f)\times\U(N_f)\to \U(N_f)$ at $\mu=1$], the interpolation is far from trivial.
nodes.statement_short: The model interpolates between GUE at $\mu=0$ and chGUE at $\mu=1$, two limits with different flavor-symmetry-breaking patterns.
conclusions: the level statistics of $\mathcal{D}$ interpolates between GUE \cite{Verbaarschot:1994ip,Mehta_book} at $\mu=0$ and chGUE~\cite{Shuryak:1992pi,Verbaarschot:1993pm,Mehta_book} at $\mu=1$.
the interpolation is far from trivial

nodes.name: Matrix dimension as spacetime volume
nodes.statement: The random matrix $\mathcal{D}$ replaces the Euclidean Dirac operator in QCD and its matrix dimension $N$ plays the role of the spacetime volume which will be eventually taken to infinity, keeping $Nm_f^2$ and $N\mu^2$ fixed.
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{D}$ stands in for the Euclidean Dirac operator and $N$ for the spacetime volume, taken to infinity at fixed $Nm_f^2$ and $N\mu^2$.

nodes.name: First application: 3d staggered fermions
nodes.statement: There are at least three major connections between the model \eqref{RMT-model} and QCD. First, \eqref{RMT-model} was proposed in~\cite{Bialas:2010hb} as a model of the 3d Dirac operator for staggered fermions.

nodes.name: Microscopic spectrum of the 3d staggered Dirac operator obeys chGUE
nodes.statement: The authors of~\cite{Bialas:2010hb} employed lattice simulations to show that the microscopic spectrum of the 3d staggered Dirac operator obeys chGUE rather than GUE due to discretization effects.
conclusions: the microscopic spectrum of the 3d staggered Dirac operator obeys chGUE rather than GUE

nodes.name: Lattice spacing modeled by the coupling $\mu$
nodes.statement: The possible convergence to GUE in the continuum limit can then be modeled by the model \eqref{RMT-model} with $\mu$ playing the role of the lattice spacing. The authors of~\cite{Bialas:2010hb} only compared Monte Carlo simulations of~\eqref{RMT-model} with lattice simulations, finding good agreement of the spectra. The microscopic level density of $\mathcal{D}$ has not been derived to date.
nodes.statement_short: $\mu$ plays the role of the lattice spacing; only Monte Carlo comparisons exist so far and the microscopic level density is still underived.

nodes.name: Second application: 4d QCD at high temperature with twisted boundary conditions
nodes.statement: Another application of \eqref{RMT-model} is to 4d QCD at high temperature with twisted fermionic boundary conditions.

nodes.name: Dimensional reduction of gauge theories at high temperature
nodes.statement: It is well known~\cite{Ginsparg:1980ef,Nadkarni:1982kb} that gauge theories at high temperature undergoes dimensional reduction.
conclusions: gauge theories at high temperature undergoes dimensional reduction

nodes.name: Avoiding chiral restoration by twisted boundary conditions along $S^1$
nodes.statement: In this regime the chiral condensate evaporates and RMT loses its validity for the infrared Dirac spectrum \cite{Kovacs:2009zj}. However, by judiciously choosing the boundary condition of quarks along $S^1$ it is possible to avoid chiral restoration up to an arbitrarily high temperature \cite{Stephanov:1996he,Bilgici:2009tx}, which has a simple explanation based on instanton-monopoles \cite{Shuryak:2012aa}.
nodes.statement_short: At high temperature the condensate evaporates, but a judicious quark boundary condition along $S^1$ postpones chiral restoration arbitrarily.
assumptions: by judiciously choosing the boundary condition of quarks along $S^1$
conclusions: it is possible to avoid chiral restoration up to an arbitrarily high temperature

nodes.name: Crossover of the smallest Dirac eigenvalues from chGUE (4d) to GUE (3d)
nodes.statement: We conjecture a crossover transition of the spectral statistics of the smallest eigenvalues of the Dirac operator from chGUE (4d) to GUE (3d).
assumptions: 4d QCD at high temperature with twisted fermionic boundary conditions
conclusions: a crossover transition of the spectral statistics of the smallest eigenvalues of the Dirac operator from chGUE (4d) to GUE (3d)

nodes.name: Euclidean Lagrangian of 3d QCD at finite isospin chemical potential
nodes.statement: The third application of the model~\eqref{RMT-model} can be found for 3d QCD at finite isospin chemical potential. The Euclidean Lagrangian is given by \begin{equation} \begin{split} \mathcal{L} = & \overline{\psi}\bigl(\mathcal{D}_{\rm 3d} + \mu_{\rm I} \sigma_3\tau_3+{\rm diag}(m_{\rm u},m_{\rm d})+j\tau_1\bigl)\psi, \end{split} \end{equation} where $\mathcal{D}_{\rm 3d}$ is the 3d Dirac operator which is anti-Hermitian, $\psi$ the two-flavor quark fields, $\mu_{\rm I}$ the isospin chemical potential, $m_{\rm u/d}$ the quark masses, $j$ the source term for the pion condensate, and $\tau_j$ and $\sigma_3$ the Pauli matrices in flavour space and spinor space, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Two-flavor 3d Euclidean Lagrangian with isospin chemical potential $\mu_{\rm I}$, quark masses, and a pion-condensate source $j$.

nodes.name: Modeling the isospin system by the two-matrix model
nodes.statement: One can model this system by the two-matrix model \eqref{eq:0Zdef} with $N_{\rm f}=1$, in close analogy to the 4d case \cite{Osborn:2004}. (Note that $j$ in \eqref{Lag-phys} corresponds to $m_f$ in \eqref{eq:0Zdef}.) The matrix model can describe the near-zero singular values of the operator ${\mathcal D}_{\rm 3d}+\mu_{\rm I}\sigma_3$ whose nonzero density at the origin is necessary to support nonzero pion condensate \cite{Kanazawa:2011tt}. The random matrix model for the Lagrangian~\eqref{Lag-phys} without the source $j$ was introduced in~\cite{Akemann:2001bf}.
nodes.statement_short: The $N_{\rm f}=1$ two-matrix model reproduces the near-zero singular values of ${\mathcal D}_{\rm 3d}+\mu_{\rm I}\sigma_3$, with $j$ playing the role of $m_f$.

nodes.name: Relation to the elliptic Ginibre ensemble
nodes.statement: The random matrix $W$ is also known as the elliptic Ginibre ensemble~\cite{Fyodorov:1997,Akemann:2001bf,Akemann:2007rf} and was studied in the scattering at disordered/chaotic systems~\cite{Fyodorov:1997b} as well as in 3d QCD at finite baryon chemical potential~\cite{Akemann:2001bf,Akemann:2007rf}. The authors of these works were interested in the complex eigenvalues of $W$ while we need the singular value statistics of $W$.

nodes.name: Bijection between singular values of $W$ and eigenvalues of $\mathcal{D}$
nodes.statement: The singular values of $W$ are bijectively related to the eigenvalues of $\mathcal{D}$ and their statistics were not calculated before.
conclusions: The singular values of $W$ are bijectively related to the eigenvalues of $\mathcal{D}$

nodes.name: Contrast with chirality-breaking Wilson Dirac random matrix models
nodes.statement: Let us mention another random matrix model for the Hermitian Wilson Dirac operator~\cite{Damgaard:2010cz,Akemann:2011} which also describes a transition between chGUE and GUE. The difference with our model is that the chirality of the random matrix is destroyed in~\cite{Damgaard:2010cz,Akemann:2011}. This has dramatic consequences for the statistics of those eigenvalues closest to the origin. When chirality is destroyed the level repulsion from the origin becomes weaker and weaker, see~\cite{Damgaard:2010cz,Akemann:2011}. This is not the case in our model where we preserve chirality. The microscopic level density will always drop to zero at the origin as long as $\mu\neq0$, see Fig.~\ref{fig.microlevel}.
nodes.statement_short: Wilson-Dirac models also cross over chGUE-GUE but destroy chirality, weakening level repulsion; here chirality is preserved so the density vanishes at the origin for $\mu\neq0$.

nodes.name: Partially quenched partition function $Z_N^{(k,N_{\rm f}+k)}$
nodes.statement: To this aim, we consider the partition function involving $k$ bosonic quarks and $N_{\rm f}+k$ fermionic quarks \begin{equation} Z_N^{(k,N_{\rm f}+k)} = \int d\mathcal{D} P(\mathcal{D})\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{N_{\rm f}+k}\det(\kappa_{{\rm f}, j} \id_{2N}+\mathcal{D})}{\prod_{j=1}^{k}\det(\kappa_{{\rm b}, j} \id_{2N}+\mathcal{D})}, \end{equation} with $k=0$ for the ordinary fermionic partition function and $k=1$ and $N_{\rm f}=0$ for the quenched microscopic level density.
nodes.statement_short: Partition function with $k$ bosonic and $N_{\rm f}+k$ fermionic quarks, reducing to the fermionic ($k=0$) and quenched ($k=1$, $N_{\rm f}=0$) cases.

nodes.name: Source variables $\kappa$
nodes.statement: The source variables are $\kappa=\diag(\kappa_{\rm b};\kappa_{\rm f})=\diag((L\epsilon-i\lambda_{\rm b})\id_k;(L\epsilon-i\lambda_{\rm f})\id_k,m_1,\ldots,m_{N_{\rm f}})$ with $m_j$ the masses of the dynamical quarks, $L=\pm1$ the sign of the regularization $\epsilon>0$ and $\lambda_{\rm b/f}$ the source variables for generating the level density.

nodes.name: Derivation of the superspace representation of the partition function
nodes.statement: In the first step we rewrite the ratio of determinants in~\eqref{eq:Zval} by a Gaussian integral over an $N\times(2k|2N_{\rm f}+2k)$ rectangular supermatrix $V$. Then the integral over $H_1$ and $H_2$ is Gaussian which can be carried out explicitly, yielding \begin{equation} \begin{split} Z_N^{(k,N_{\rm f}+k)} = \; &\frac{1}{\pi^{2 Nk}}\int dV \exp\big[\! -L\; \Str\,V^\dagger V\kappa \\ &-\Str (V^\dagger V\tau_1)^2/2-\mu^2\Str (V^\dagger V\tau_2)^2/2 \big]. \end{split} \end{equation} For the definition of the supertrace and other objects in superspace like the superdeterminant we refer the reader to~\cite{Berezin}. Note that we suppress the tensor notation with identity matrices meaning $\kappa$ has to be understood in the $(2k|2N_{\rm f}+2k)$ dimensional superspace as $\kappa\otimes\id_2$ and the Pauli matrices $\tau_j$ as $\id_{k|N_{\rm f}+k}\otimes\tau_j$. In the next step we apply the superbosonization formula~\cite{Zirnbauer:2006,Kieburg:2008} and replace \begin{equation} LV^\dagger V\tau_1\rightarrow \sqrt{N} U'=\sqrt{N}\left(\begin{array}{cc} U'_{\rm bb} & \eta^\dagger \\ \eta & U'_{\rm ff} \end{array}\right), \end{equation} where the the boson-boson block $U'_{\rm bb}$ satisfies $LU'_{\rm bb}\tau_1=(LU'_{\rm bb}\tau_1)^\dagger>0$ and the fermion-fermion block $U'_{\rm ff}$ is unitary. The $2k\times(2k|2N_{\rm f}+2k)$ off-diagonal block $\eta$ comprises only independent complex Grassmann variables.
nodes.statement_short: Linearize the determinant ratio by a Gaussian supermatrix integral, integrate out $H_1,H_2$, then superbosonize $LV^\dagger V\tau_1\to\sqrt{N}U'$.

nodes.name: Superbosonized form of the partition function
nodes.statement: In terms of this supermatrix, the partition function is up to a global constant equal to \begin{equation} \begin{split} Z_N^{(k_{\rm b},k_{\rm f})} \propto& \int d\tilde{\mu}(U')\; \Sdet^{N}U' \exp\big[\!-\Str\,U'\widehat{\kappa}\tau_1 \\ & - N\, \Str\,{U'}^2/2 + \widehat{\mu}^2\Str (U'\tau_3)^2/2 \big]. \end{split} \end{equation} Here we have already chosen the rescaling from the $\epsilon$-regime, namely $\widehat{\kappa}=\sqrt{N}\kappa$ and $\widehat{\mu}^2=N\mu^2$ which are fixed in the large-$N$ limit.
nodes.statement_short: After superbosonization the partition function becomes a supermatrix integral over $U'$ with weight $\Sdet^N U'$ and rescaled sources $\widehat{\kappa},\widehat{\mu}$.
assumptions: Here we have already chosen the rescaling from the $\epsilon$-regime, namely $\widehat{\kappa}=\sqrt{N}\kappa$ and $\widehat{\mu}^2=N\mu^2$

nodes.name: Monte Carlo check of the quenched microscopic level density
nodes.statement: Comparison of the analytical result~\eqref{level.density} (red solid curves) for the quenched microscopic level density with Monte Carlo simulations (blue square markers) of the random matrix model~\eqref{RMT-model} for several couplings $\widehat{\mu}$. The ensemble was generated with $10^5$ matrices and the matrix size is $n=100$ apart from plot (a) where it is $n=200$ because the effect of a finite matrix dimension is strongest there. The dashed black curves in (a) and (d) are the limiting microscopic level densities for $\widehat{\mu}\to\infty$ (chGUE) and for $\widehat{\mu}\to0$ (GUE), respectively. The normalization is given by $\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\rho(\lambda)=2/\pi$.
nodes.statement_short: Analytical density compared with $10^5$-matrix Monte Carlo ensembles at several $\widehat{\mu}$, against the chGUE and GUE limiting curves.

nodes.name: Derivation of the chiral Lagrangian in the large-$N$ limit
nodes.statement: First we want to consider the partition function with $N_{\rm f}$ dynamical quarks, i.e. $k=0$ \cite{comm}. There is no supersymmetry and the whole supermatrix consists of the fermion-fermion block, only, $U'=U_{\rm ff}$. For $N\to\infty$ we have to solve the saddle point equation \begin{equation} U'^2=\id_{2N_{\rm f}}. \end{equation} This implies that all eigenvalues of $U'$ are $\pm1$. When diagonalizing $U'$ to its eigenvalues $e^{i \phi}=\diag(e^{i \phi_1},\ldots,e^{i \phi_{N_{\rm f}}})$ we would obtain the Vandermonde term $|\Delta_{N_{\rm f}}(e^{i \phi})|^2=\prod_{a<b}|e^{i \phi_b}-e^{i \phi_a}|^2$ as the Jacobian. This term algebraically suppresses all solutions of~\eqref{sad.eq} in $1/N$ which do not have an equal number of $\pm1$. Thus we integrate only over the coset ${\rm U}(2N_{\rm f})/[{\rm U}(N_{\rm f})\times {\rm U}(N_{\rm f})]$ which is the same as for $\mu=0$ (GUE, 3d QCD), see~\cite{Verbaarschot:1994ip}. This coset can be parametrized as $U'=U\tau_3 U^\dagger$ with $U\in{\rm U}(2N_{\rm f})$.
nodes.statement_short: Saddle-point analysis at $k=0$: the Vandermonde Jacobian suppresses unbalanced $\pm1$ solutions, leaving the coset ${\rm U}(2N_{\rm f})/[{\rm U}(N_{\rm f})\times{\rm U}(N_{\rm f})]$.

nodes.name: Saddle point equation
nodes.statement: For $N\to\infty$ we have to solve the saddle point equation \begin{equation} U'^2=\id_{2N_{\rm f}}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Chiral Lagrangian: large-$N$ partition function with $N_{\rm f}$ flavors
nodes.statement: The chiral Lagrangian contains a perturbation to the $\widehat{\mu}=0$ result~\cite{Verbaarschot:1994ip,Szabo:2005gi} and the partition function in the large-$N$ limit is given as \begin{align} Z^{(0,N_{\rm f})}=\!\!\!\!\! \int\limits_{\U(2N_{\rm f})} \!\!\!\!\!\! d\mu(U)\exp\left[\tr\,U\tau_3U^\dagger \widehat{\kappa}\tau_1-\frac{\widehat{\mu}^2}{2}\tr(U\tau_3U^\dagger\tau_3)^2\right]\!. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: The large-$N$ partition function is a ${\rm U}(2N_{\rm f})$ integral with the usual mass term plus a $\widehat{\mu}^2$ crossover term.
assumptions: the partition function with $N_{\rm f}$ dynamical quarks, i.e. $k=0$
The chiral Lagrangian contains a perturbation to the $\widehat{\mu}=0$ result~\cite{Verbaarschot:1994ip,Szabo:2005gi}

nodes.name: Symmetry crossover controlled by the $\widehat{\mu}^2$ term
nodes.statement: The symmetry crossover is controlled by the second term. It gives nonzero masses to splitt off the Nambu-Goldstone modes, reducing the coset down to $\U(N_{\rm f})$ for large $\widehat{\mu}$. We expect that the result \eqref{k-flav-f} reproduces the leading order of the $\epsilon$-expansion in QCD for the three areas of applications discussed above.
nodes.statement_short: The $\widehat{\mu}^2$ term gives mass to Nambu-Goldstone modes and reduces the coset to $\U(N_{\rm f})$ at large $\widehat{\mu}$.

nodes.name: Pfaffian determinant form of the $N_{\rm f}$-flavor partition function
nodes.statement: In~\cite{Kanazawa:2018b} we have even carried out the integral over $U$ explicitly, which yielded either an $N_{\rm f}\times N_{\rm f}$ or an $(N_{\rm f}+1)\times(N_{\rm f}+1)$ Pfaffian determinant, depending on whether $N_{\rm f}$ is even or odd, respectively. This Pfaffian structure was also obtained in finite $N$ computations by us in~\cite{Kanazawa:2018a}.
assumptions: depending on whether $N_{\rm f}$ is even or odd, respectively
conclusions: which yielded either an $N_{\rm f}\times N_{\rm f}$ or an $(N_{\rm f}+1)\times(N_{\rm f}+1)$ Pfaffian determinant

nodes.name: Microscopic level density from the partially quenched partition function
nodes.statement: Next we want to derive the microscopic level density in the quenched limit. Its relation to the partially quenched partition function for $k=1$ and $N_{\rm f}=0$ is \begin{equation} \rho(\lambda)=\frac{1}{\pi}\lim_{\epsilon\to0}{\rm Re}\left.\partial_{\widehat{\kappa}_{\rm f}}Z_N^{(1,1)}\right|_{\widehat{\kappa}_{\rm b}=\widehat{\kappa}_{\rm f}=L\epsilon-i \lambda}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The quenched level density is the regularized real part of a $\widehat{\kappa}_{\rm f}$-derivative of $Z_N^{(1,1)}$.

nodes.name: Derivation of the quenched microscopic level density
nodes.statement:
In the large-$N$ limit the saddle point equation~\eqref{sad.eq} still applies though with a different dimension in the unit matrix. For this reason we use the parametrization  egin{equation}  egin{split} {U'}_{m bb}& = Le^{-\vartheta_1	au_3/2}e^{-\vartheta_2	au_2/2}	au_1e^{z_1\id_2+z_2 	au_1}e^{\vartheta_2	au_2/2}e^{\vartheta_1	au_3/2},\ {U'}_{m ff}& = e^{-i\varphi_1	au_3/2}e^{-i\varphi_2	au_2/2}	au_1e^{i(z_3\id_2+z_4 	au_1)}e^{i\varphi_2	au_2/2}e^{i\varphi_1	au_3/2}, \end{split} \end{equation} for the two diagonal blocks of $U'$. The angles take the values $z_1,z_2,\vartheta_1,\vartheta_2\in\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi_1\in[-\pi,\pi]$, and $\varphi_2,z_3,z_4\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$. From the saddle point equation and the properties of ${U'}_{m bb}$ and ${U'}_{m ff}$ we have to expand the variables $z_j$ as follows: $(z_1,z_2)=(\delta z_1/\sqrt{N},\delta z_2/\sqrt{N})$ and $(z_3,z_4)=(\delta z_3/\sqrt{N},$ $\delta z_4/\sqrt{N}), ~(z_3,z_4)=(\pi/2+\delta z_3/\sqrt{N},\pi/2+\delta z_4/\sqrt{N})$. The latter expansion for $z_3,z_4$ yields an algebraically $1/N$-suppressed term. The expansion to leading order in $1/N$ and integration over $\eta$ and $\delta z_j$ is quite lengthy and we omit it here. It is done in detail in~\cite{Kanazawa:2018b}. Afterwards we integrate over $\varphi_1$ and $\vartheta_1$ which yields the modified Bessel functions of first order, $I_j$, and of second order, $K_j$, respectively. Then we are able to use the relation~\eqref{level-part}. nodes.statement:

assumptions: $k=1$ and $N_{\rm f}=0$ for the quenched microscopic level density

nodes.name: Non-uniform GUE limit due to preserved chirality
nodes.statement: This density is plotted in Fig.~\ref{fig.microlevel} and compared with Monte Carlo simulations of the random matrix model~\eqref{RMT-model} for several $\widehat{\mu}$. One immediately notices the different behaviour of this result compared to the one in~\cite{Damgaard:2010cz,Akemann:2011}, where the transition between chGUE and GUE was done in a way which breaks chirality, reflecting the form of the Wilson Dirac operator. Due to the preservation of chirality in our model, the GUE limit ($\widehat{\mu}\to0$) is not uniform about the origin while it is in~\cite{Damgaard:2010cz,Akemann:2011} when the quark mass vanishes. As we have already pointed out, an exact chirality yields for a complex matrix a linear level repulsion from the origin, though the range where this is happening is of order $\mathcal{O}(\widehat{\mu})$ for small $\widehat{\mu}$. However the two models also have something in common. The oscillations are increasingly suppressed when $\widehat{\mu}$ decreases, whereas the limit $\widehat{\mu}\to\infty$ to the chGUE result is uniformly approached.
nodes.statement_short: Preserved chirality makes the $\widehat{\mu}\to0$ GUE limit non-uniform at the origin, while the $\widehat{\mu}\to\infty$ chGUE limit is uniform.

nodes.name: Summary of the derivations and their significance
nodes.statement: We sketched the derivation of the chiral Lagrangian, see Eq.~\eqref{k-flav-f}, and the microscopic level density, see Eq.~\eqref{level.density}, in the $\epsilon$-regime of QCD for the random matrix model~\eqref{RMT-model} which interpolates between chGUE ($=$ 4d continuum QCD) and GUE ($=$ 3d continuum QCD). The details of these computations are done in~\cite{Kanazawa:2018b} and finite $N$ results are given in~\cite{Kanazawa:2018a}. Again, we underline that the crucial difference with the related models in~\cite{Damgaard:2010cz,Akemann:2011} is the preservation of chirality which has drastic consequences on the eigenvalues close to the origin. However we do not expect any differences for the spectral statistics in the bulk and at the soft edges.
nodes.statement_short: The chiral Lagrangian and the level density were derived for the chGUE-GUE interpolation; only the near-origin eigenvalues differ from chirality-breaking models.

nodes.name: Generalizations to dynamical quarks and higher correlations
nodes.statement: The results we presented here can be readily generalized to the situation of $N_{\rm f}$ dynamical quarks as well as to higher order correlation functions.

nodes.name: Pfaffian point process for the spectral statistics
nodes.statement: In~\cite{Kanazawa:2018a} we have shown that the spectral statistics describe a Pfaffian point process meaning that all $k$-point correlation functions as well as averages over ratios of characteristic polynomials of the random matrix $\mathcal{D}$ are given by Pfaffian determinants which only comprise three functions.
nodes.statement_short: All $k$-point functions and characteristic-polynomial ratios of $\mathcal{D}$ are Pfaffians built from just three kernel functions.
conclusions: the spectral statistics describe a Pfaffian point process

nodes.name: Physical Dirac operators should follow the same Pfaffian point process
nodes.statement: In particular the statistics of the infra-red eigenvalues of the physical Dirac operators in QCD (say 3d staggered Dirac operators or 3d continuum theory with isospin chemical potential) should also follow this Pfaffian point process and all the consequences related to it.
assumptions: the statistics of the infra-red eigenvalues of the physical Dirac operators in QCD
conclusions: should also follow this Pfaffian point process

nodes.name: Relevance beyond QCD
nodes.statement: Given the connection of RMT to various fields of physics we anticipate that the solution presented in the present work would be of value outside of QCD as well, especially in the field of condensed matter systems with emergent Dirac fermions.

nodes.name: Linearize the determinant ratio with a supermatrix
nodes.statement: In the first step we rewrite the ratio of determinants in~\eqref{eq:Zval} by a Gaussian integral over an $N\times(2k|2N_{\rm f}+2k)$ rectangular supermatrix $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce a rectangular supermatrix $V$ to write the ratio of determinants as a Gaussian integral.

nodes.name: Carry out the Gaussian integral over $H_1$ and $H_2$
nodes.statement: Then the integral over $H_1$ and $H_2$ is Gaussian which can be carried out explicitly, yielding \begin{equation} \begin{split} Z_N^{(k,N_{\rm f}+k)} = \; &\frac{1}{\pi^{2 Nk}}\int dV \exp\big[\! -L\; \Str\,V^\dagger V\kappa \\ &-\Str (V^\dagger V\tau_1)^2/2-\mu^2\Str (V^\dagger V\tau_2)^2/2 \big]. \end{split} \end{equation} For the definition of the supertrace and other objects in superspace like the superdeterminant we refer the reader to~\cite{Berezin}. Note that we suppress the tensor notation with identity matrices meaning $\kappa$ has to be understood in the $(2k|2N_{\rm f}+2k)$ dimensional superspace as $\kappa\otimes\id_2$ and the Pauli matrices $\tau_j$ as $\id_{k|N_{\rm f}+k}\otimes\tau_j$.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate out the two Hermitian matrices, leaving a quartic supermatrix integral over $V$.

nodes.name: Apply the superbosonization formula
nodes.statement: In the next step we apply the superbosonization formula~\cite{Zirnbauer:2006,Kieburg:2008} and replace \begin{equation} LV^\dagger V\tau_1\rightarrow \sqrt{N} U'=\sqrt{N}\left(\begin{array}{cc} U'_{\rm bb} & \eta^\dagger \\ \eta & U'_{\rm ff} \end{array}\right), \end{equation} where the the boson-boson block $U'_{\rm bb}$ satisfies $LU'_{\rm bb}\tau_1=(LU'_{\rm bb}\tau_1)^\dagger>0$ and the fermion-fermion block $U'_{\rm ff}$ is unitary. The $2k\times(2k|2N_{\rm f}+2k)$ off-diagonal block $\eta$ comprises only independent complex Grassmann variables.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $LV^\dagger V\tau_1$ by $\sqrt{N}U'$ with a positive boson-boson block, a unitary fermion-fermion block, and Grassmann off-diagonals.

nodes.name: Specialize to the purely fermionic case $k=0$
nodes.statement: First we want to consider the partition function with $N_{\rm f}$ dynamical quarks, i.e. $k=0$ \cite{comm}. There is no supersymmetry and the whole supermatrix consists of the fermion-fermion block, only, $U'=U_{\rm ff}$.
nodes.statement_short: Set $k=0$, so the supermatrix reduces to its fermion-fermion block.

nodes.name: Solve the saddle point equation
nodes.statement: For $N\to\infty$ we have to solve the saddle point equation \begin{equation} U'^2=\id_{2N_{\rm f}}. \end{equation} This implies that all eigenvalues of $U'$ are $\pm1$.
nodes.statement_short: The large-$N$ saddle point forces all eigenvalues of $U'$ to be $\pm1$.

nodes.name: Vandermonde Jacobian suppresses unbalanced saddles
nodes.statement: When diagonalizing $U'$ to its eigenvalues $e^{i \phi}=\diag(e^{i \phi_1},\ldots,e^{i \phi_{N_{\rm f}}})$ we would obtain the Vandermonde term $|\Delta_{N_{\rm f}}(e^{i \phi})|^2=\prod_{a<b}|e^{i \phi_b}-e^{i \phi_a}|^2$ as the Jacobian. This term algebraically suppresses all solutions of~\eqref{sad.eq} in $1/N$ which do not have an equal number of $\pm1$.
nodes.statement_short: The Vandermonde Jacobian suppresses in $1/N$ every saddle without equally many $+1$ and $-1$ eigenvalues.

nodes.name: Reduce the integral to the Goldstone coset
nodes.statement: Thus we integrate only over the coset ${\rm U}(2N_{\rm f})/[{\rm U}(N_{\rm f})\times {\rm U}(N_{\rm f})]$ which is the same as for $\mu=0$ (GUE, 3d QCD), see~\cite{Verbaarschot:1994ip}. This coset can be parametrized as $U'=U\tau_3 U^\dagger$ with $U\in{\rm U}(2N_{\rm f})$.
nodes.statement_short: Only the coset ${\rm U}(2N_{\rm f})/[{\rm U}(N_{\rm f})\times{\rm U}(N_{\rm f})]$ survives, parametrized by $U'=U\tau_3U^\dagger$.

nodes.name: Parametrize the diagonal blocks of $U'$
nodes.statement: In the large-$N$ limit the saddle point equation~\eqref{sad.eq} still applies though with a different dimension in the unit matrix. For this reason we use the parametrization \begin{equation} \begin{split} {U'}_{\rm bb}& = Le^{-\vartheta_1\tau_3/2}e^{-\vartheta_2\tau_2/2}\tau_1e^{z_1\id_2+z_2 \tau_1}e^{\vartheta_2\tau_2/2}e^{\vartheta_1\tau_3/2},\\ {U'}_{\rm ff}& = e^{-i\varphi_1\tau_3/2}e^{-i\varphi_2\tau_2/2}\tau_1e^{i(z_3\id_2+z_4 \tau_1)}e^{i\varphi_2\tau_2/2}e^{i\varphi_1\tau_3/2}, \end{split} \end{equation} for the two diagonal blocks of $U'$. The angles take the values $z_1,z_2,\vartheta_1,\vartheta_2\in\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi_1\in[-\pi,\pi]$, and $\varphi_2,z_3,z_4\in[-\pi/2,\pi/2]$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce angular coordinates for the boson-boson and fermion-fermion blocks with their integration ranges.

nodes.name: Expand the radial variables around the saddle points
nodes.statement: From the saddle point equation and the properties of ${U'}_{\rm bb}$ and ${U'}_{\rm ff}$ we have to expand the variables $z_j$ as follows: $(z_1,z_2)=(\delta z_1/\sqrt{N},\delta z_2/\sqrt{N})$ and $(z_3,z_4)=(\delta z_3/\sqrt{N},$ $\delta z_4/\sqrt{N}), ~(z_3,z_4)=(\pi/2+\delta z_3/\sqrt{N},\pi/2+\delta z_4/\sqrt{N})$. The latter expansion for $z_3,z_4$ yields an algebraically $1/N$-suppressed term.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale $z_j$ by $1/\sqrt{N}$ around both saddle points, the shifted one being $1/N$-suppressed.

nodes.name: Perform the (omitted) leading-order expansion and Grassmann integration
nodes.statement: The expansion to leading order in $1/N$ and integration over $\eta$ and $\delta z_j$ is quite lengthy and we omit it here. It is done in detail in~\cite{Kanazawa:2018b}.
nodes.statement_short: The lengthy leading-order expansion and $\eta$, $\delta z_j$ integrations are deferred to the companion paper.

nodes.name: Integrate over the remaining angles to get Bessel functions
nodes.statement: Afterwards we integrate over $\varphi_1$ and $\vartheta_1$ which yields the modified Bessel functions of first order, $I_j$, and of second order, $K_j$, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Integrating $\varphi_1$ and $\vartheta_1$ produces the Bessel functions $I_j$ and $K_j$.

nodes.name: Use the level-density relation and a Bessel identity

nodes.statement_short: Apply the level-density relation and the $\epsilon\to0$ Bessel identity turning $K_\nu$ into $J_\nu$.
